content_voiceover: This is a high-yield board fact. Hemophilia severity is classified by residual clotting factor activity, and it correlates closely with clinical bleeding phenotype. Severe hemophilia is defined as less than one percent factor activity, and these patients have spontaneous bleeding into joints and muscles, even without trauma. Moderate hemophilia falls between one and five percent factor activity, and bleeding usually occurs after relatively minor trauma or surgery, with occasional spontaneous episodes. Mild hemophilia covers five up to forty percent factor activity, and these patients often go undiagnosed for years because they only bleed with major trauma, surgery, or dental procedures. Knowing these cutoffs is essential, because they directly predict a patient's bleeding risk and guide decisions about prophylactic factor replacement before procedures.
keypoints: Severe disease means under 1% factor activity, with spontaneous joint and muscle bleeding
Moderate disease means 1 to 5% factor activity, bleeding after minor trauma
Mild disease means 5 to 40% factor activity, bleeding mainly with major trauma or surgery
Severity level predicts bleeding risk and guides prophylaxis decisions
keypoint_voiceover: Remember these three tiers. Severe is under one percent activity with spontaneous bleeds, moderate is one to five percent with trauma-related bleeding, and mild is five to forty percent, often only bleeding with surgery or major injury. These cutoffs are classic board material, so know them cold.
